opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to a few things.

First, context is just incredibly cheap and flexible. When you put something into the context window, you get this immediate, inspectable, reversible kind of customization. You can see exactly what the model is conditioning on, you can edit it, you can swap it out per user or per task, and the model is already very good at in-context learning because that's basically what pretraining optimized for. So it's a very natural knob to turn.

Weights are a totally different story. When you change the weights, you're doing surgery on this giant, entangled, distributed representation. Knowledge and capability aren't stored in neat little boxes; they're smeared across billions of parameters. So if you fine-tune on your narrow domain, you can get what you want, but you often also get regressions elsewhere. Catastrophic forgetting is still a real thing, and you lose some of the general capability that made the model valuable in the first place. It's hard to add a skill without subtly breaking ten other things you weren't measuring.

Then there's the practical side. Fine-tuning needs data pipelines, evals, compute, and expertise, and every time the base model improves, which happens every few months, your specialization is kind of stranded on an old checkpoint. Meanwhile, your prompt or your retrieved context just carries over to the new model for free. So economically, a lot of people rationally choose context.

And I think there's a deeper point, which is that we don't really have a good analog of how humans consolidate memory. A person learns something during the day, it lives in working memory, and then somehow, maybe during sleep, it gets distilled into the weights, in a way that doesn't wreck everything else. We don't have that process for LLMs. We have the context window, which is like working memory, and we have the weights, which get set during this huge pretraining run, and there's not a great continuous, graceful mechanism in between. That's an open research problem, and I'd expect it to be one of the more interesting areas over the next few years: some kind of continual learning or distillation that lets models actually internalize what they experience, rather than us constantly re-stuffing the context window.

r001.rationale: It calls catastrophic forgetting a real issue and says fine-tuning can cause regressions that reduce the model’s general capabilities, presenting this as unresolved.

r002.rationale: It explains that changing entangled weights can cause regressions elsewhere and subtly break capabilities beyond the specialization.

r003.rationale: It cites the practical costs of fine-tuning and says people often choose context customization for economic reasons, conveying that weight-based specialization must be cost-effective.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't actually have a good story for how to do it yet. When you put something in the context window, you're basically using the model's in-context learning ability, and that ability is a very general, very robust thing that fell out of pretraining. The model has seen so much text that it has learned how to pick up on patterns in its context and continue them. It's a kind of meta-learning that's just baked in. So you give it a few examples, you give it some documents, you give it instructions, and it adapts on the fly. And crucially, it does that without touching anything that's load-bearing. The weights are frozen, so you're not going to break anything.

Fine-tuning is a very different beast. When you change the weights, you're reaching into this very high-dimensional, very delicately balanced object and nudging it, and you don't really know what else you're nudging along the way. There's this problem people call catastrophic forgetting, which is a bit dramatic as a name, but the underlying thing is real. You train on your specialized dataset, and the model gets better at that thing, and then you discover it's gotten a little dumber at a bunch of other things that you didn't measure. The capabilities in these networks are entangled. They're not in neat little modules you can swap out. So you end up in this regime where you need a lot of care around the data mix, you need regularization, you need to replay some of the original distribution, and even then you're kind of flying blind because evaluating the full capability surface of a model is really hard.

There's also just a data issue. In-context learning works with very little. You can show it three examples. To fine-tune well, you typically need a lot more than that, and it needs to be high quality, and it needs to be formatted the right way, and most people who want a specialized model don't have that. So the economics of it are kind of bad. You spend a lot of effort on data curation and training infrastructure to get something that you could have gotten, maybe eighty percent of the way, by just writing a good prompt and stuffing the right documents in.

And I think the deeper thing, the thing that I find kind of interesting, is that we don't have a good analog of what humans do. A person reads a book and some of it gets consolidated into long-term knowledge, and we don't really know how to do that for these models. The context window is like working memory. It's fast and flexible and it disappears. The weights are like long-term memory, but our only tool for writing to them is gradient descent on big batches of data, which is a very blunt instrument. There's no mechanism for the model to reflect on what happened today and distill the useful parts into itself in some surgical way. People are working on this, and I think it's one of the more important open problems, but right now context is just the easier lever to pull because it's the one that actually works reliably.

r001.rationale: The response calls reliable weight-based specialization an unresolved problem and describes fine-tuning as improving one task while potentially degrading other capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says weight changes can make the model “a little dumber at a bunch of other things,” communicating effects on its broader capabilities.

r003.rationale: It describes fine-tuning’s data and infrastructure costs as making its economics poor compared with prompting, communicating that the cost must be worthwhile for the use.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is that context is a very direct way to program the model. You put the information in there, and the model can immediately use it. You can inspect it, change it, take something out. And the model has been trained extensively to condition on that context.

With weights, you’re trying to get that information into this enormous, distributed representation through optimization. That’s a much less direct interface. If I give you a document and fine-tune on it, it’s not obvious that the model will internalize all the facts, or be able to access them in all the ways I might want. The training objective and the capability you’re trying to create don’t necessarily line up that neatly.

And then you have to worry about what else changed. Did you improve the specialized task but degrade something else? Did you overfit to the examples? So there’s a whole training and evaluation loop involved.

I don’t think that means specialization through weights won’t work. It’s just that, today, putting the right information in context is much easier to control. You’re giving the model working material, whereas changing the weights is trying to teach it a lasting skill. We have a much more straightforward interface for the former.

r001.rationale: It describes the risk that fine-tuning improves a specialized task while degrading other capabilities, framing this as an ongoing concern.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible degradation elsewhere but does not say weight changes can affect the model’s overall intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the cost of weight-based specialization or whether it is affordable for its intended use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big difference is that the context window is this very explicit working memory. You can put in documents, examples, instructions, and the model can immediately condition on them. You can inspect what you put there, change it, remove it. It’s a fairly straightforward interface.

With the weights, you’re trying to take that information and bake it into this enormous distributed representation. And the interface for doing that is much less direct. You need a training objective, you need data, you need to choose how much to train. Then you have to ask: Did it actually learn the thing? Will it generalize? Did we damage some other capability in the process?

There’s also a difference between knowing something and being able to learn it from a document. If you put a document in context, the model can refer back to it while answering. If you train on that document, you’re asking it to reconstruct the relevant information from its parameters later. Those aren’t equivalent operations.

So I don’t think specialization through weights is fundamentally impossible. We do it. But context is currently a much easier mechanism to program and debug. The interesting question is how to make updating the weights feel more like learning: you give the system some experience, it incorporates that experience reliably, and you don’t have to become a training expert every time.

r001.rationale: The response describes weight training as difficult to verify and says it may damage other capabilities, identifying preservation of existing capabilities as an unresolved challenge.

r002.rationale: It says training can damage another capability, communicating that changing weights can affect capabilities beyond the intended specialization.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss the cost of weight-based specialization or whether it is inexpensive enough to be worthwhile.
